pr_title: Make hooks/middleware run in the order in which they are defined

issue_context.title: Consider using `.after()` inside `.addHook` and `.use` calls
comments: I think this is a good idea. @delvedor what do you think?
Makes sense to me.

It is ok for me.

**NB:** In the "hook pattern", each listener has to be independent from each other.

I've been trying to implement this and now I have a question.

Since this change means that handlers—and not-found handlers—will only run hooks/middleware that are defined before the handler, what do we do about the default not-found handler? Currently it gets set when the `fastify` instance is created, which means that it won't run any hooks or middleware. Is that okay? Or should we make it a special case and allow all non-encapsulated hooks and middleware to run before it?

The decision on this would solve this current issue:

```js
const fastify = require('fastify')()

fastify.register(require('a-plugin-with-a-preHandler'))

fastify.addHook('preHandler', function preHandlerA (request, reply, next) {
  request.preHandlerA = true
  next()
})

fastify.listen()
```

The default not-found handler will have `preHandlerA` run before it, but not the `preHandler` from the plugin.

> Since this change means that handlers—and not-found handlers—will only run hooks/middleware that are defined before the handler, what do we do about the default not-found handler? Currently it gets set when the fastify instance is created, which means that it won't run any hooks or middleware. Is that okay? Or should we make it a special case and allow all non-encapsulated hooks and middleware to run before it?

I don't think this should be the correct plan, ideally all hooks and middlewares defined "at the same level" should all be executed. I think we might want to keep things the way we are for 1.0.0, and rethink the encapsulation model a bit for 2.0.0.
In that case, we'll need to document the `fastify.after()` method.

I agree that we should update the docs and make a recommendation on how register the components of the application.

```
plugins (cookies, compression...)
decorators
routes (could be also a plugin)
```

I'll work on this.
Regarding the internal usage of `after` to register hooks and middlewares I'm 👍 .

ps: the `BDA` order is correct, because we `push` the new hooks, ands register are executed after the current sync context.
The second register (`C`) will not work because an `after` function runs *always* after previous one declared `register`.

@delvedor If we internally use `after` when registering hooks and middleware then the result of my example will be `AB`. I think this would be a better developer experience because linear ordering is easier to work with (it's also similar to how Express and Koa register middleware), but I'm wondering if you agree?

I think we might want to improve a bit the situation. Instead of generating an hook and middleware runner for every route, we should generate them for every plugin, after the plugin has finished loading. This should solve most of the issues. I remember we implemented them in this way in the beginning, but I do not remember why we changed them.

> Basically we should popolate the context object and register the routes only at the end of the plugin work (how will this work top level?).

No. I mean that the route context links to a plugin context, which includes all those details which will be shared.

@mcollina That makes sense (generating hooks/middleware for each Fastify instance instead of each route). It was probably changed because of non-encapsulated plugins:

```js
fastify.register(require('plugin-1'))

fastify.get('/1', ...) // has only plugin-1

fastify.register(require('plugin-2'))

fastify.get('/2', ...) // has plugin-1 and plugin-2
```

They're all at the same level, but `plugin-2` gets registered after the `get('/1')` route is already set up.

@mcollina A solution would be to have hooks/middlware use `after` and then have routes use `ready`. That way, routes will be set up once all of the plugins/hooks/middleware for the Fastify instance are ready. However, this is only possible if `ready` doesn't automatically start the boot process.

Also for future reference, this solution would cause the result of my [earlier example](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/issues/748#issuecomment-362954220) to be `ABCD`.
Let’s just document what we have and ship 1.0.0. Then we can focus on this issue

This was regressed in https://github.com/fastify/fastify/pull/474. This is caused by the hookRunner (and before that fast-iterator) creating a closure inside `.after` from within `.route`. Note that this happens only when plugins are involved, otherwise after takes care of them.

This is a test that reproduces the problem:

```
diff --git a/test/hooks.test.js b/test/hooks.test.js
index c0f00e6..6db8f38 100644
--- a/test/hooks.test.js
+++ b/test/hooks.test.js
@@ -6,6 +6,7 @@ const sget = require('simple-get').concat
 const stream = require('stream')
 const Fastify = require('..')
 const fs = require('fs')
+const fp = require('fastify-plugin')

 const payload = { hello: 'world' }

@@ -1252,3 +1253,44 @@ if (Number(process.versions.node[0]) >= 8) {
   t.pass('Skip because Node version < 8')
   t.end()
 }
+
+test('Register an hook after a plugin', t => {
+  t.plan(6)
+  const fastify = Fastify()
+
+  fastify.register(fp(function (instance, opts, next) {
+    instance.addHook('preHandler', function (req, reply, next) {
+      t.ok('called')
+      next()
+    })
+
+    instance.get('/', function (request, reply) {
+      reply.send({ hello: 'world' })
+    })
+
+    next()
+  }))
+
+  fastify.register(fp(function (instance, opts, next) {
+    fastify.addHook('preHandler', function (req, reply, next) {
+      t.ok('called')
+      next()
+    })
+
+    fastify.addHook('preHandler', function (req, reply, next) {
+      t.ok('called')
+      next()
+    })
+
+    next()
+  }))
+
+  fastify.inject({
+    url: '/',
+    method: 'GET'
+  }, (err, res) => {
+    t.error(err)
+    t.is(res.statusCode, 200)
+    t.deepEqual(JSON.parse(res.payload), { hello: 'world' })
+  })
+})
```

The problem is generated here:
https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/efc4525236b1d2831521fd3735001d110efc83dd/fastify.js#L490

Since we use concat we loose the reference to the instance hooks and we don't get any further updates. If you run the same test with `onRequest` everything will work as expected.
I'll work on a solution.
Closed by #762.
With the fix from #762 the result of my [example](#issuecomment-362954220) will be `BDAC`. @delvedor are you no longer interested in using `after` to make the result `ABCD`?
Currently I have no time for that, but if you can, fire a pr! :)

review_comments: while we are changing this, how about we move `_hooks` to `Symbol('hooks')` as well?

I'm not sure about this. If we use a Symbol for `_hooks`, should we do the same for `_middlewares` as well? Should we change all `fastify._*` property keys to Symbols? Or is there a specific reason why some keys should be a Symbol and some should be an underscore `_*`?

As long as all the property with Symbols are only used during the initial phase is ok. If we are using that property during the normal lifecycle of Fastify, I prefer we use classic objects keys, since they are slightly faster.

Almost all of the `fastify._*` properties are only used during the initial startup phase, so should we use Symbols for all of them? I think keeping them as a regular string key is helpful for debugging: `console.log(fastify._hooks)`. But if we want to use Symbols, I think it would be better to do that in a separate PR. Changing `_hooks` here would create 14 lines of changes that are completely unrelated to the goal of this PR.

@nwoltman This test checks the hook order. The second hook preHandler is called before the first one. Why? 

Both of preHabdler hooks are been registered inside a plugin

The "second" `preHandler` hook is called first because it is registered inside a non-encapsulated plugin (using `fp`) so it is registered on the root Fastify instance, which is the parent of the first (encapsulated) plugin. Hooks defined on a parent instance are always called before the hooks in a child instance.

It's the same as if the second `preHandler` hooks was defined in the same place, but not inside a plugin.
